source: Hualde, José I. & Jon Ortiz de Urbina (eds.). 2003. A Grammar of Basque. De Gruyter Mouton.
claim: The grammar's phonology chapter comprises segmental phonology (pp.15–64), accentuation (65–71), and intonation (72–112); modern Standard Basque is the focus but dialectal data and historical periods are included.
The native/established onset clusters allowed are muta-cum-liquida types, including fl- and fr- but excluding dl- and tl-.

Stop+liquid onset clusters were absent at older stages; Latin/early Romance borrowings show stop deletion or vowel epenthesis, while many modern clusters reflect more recent borrowing or native syncope.
Basque has no syllabic consonants; only vowels and diphthongs may form syllable nuclei.
Word-internal codas may be a place-assimilated nasal, a liquid, or a sibilant fricative; certain nasal/liquid+sibilant coda groups occur at morpheme boundaries.

Stops and affricates are not allowed in word-internal codas; in morphologically complex words preconsonantal stops delete and affricates reduce to fricatives, with comparable adaptation in established borrowings.
Rhotics are excluded word-initially except in very recent technical loans; integrated rhotic-initial loans generally receive a prothetic vowel.
Initial ts and tz are extremely restricted; tz occurs in some eastern expressive/augmentative forms and ts is essentially absent word-initially aside from marginal technical borrowing.
Intervocalically the voiced/voiceless stop contrast is maintained, but phonemic voiced stops are realized as weak fricatives or approximants rather than stops.
The voicing contrast in stops is neutralized word-finally; only final -k and -t occur, with some dialects allowing voiced-approximant realizations of the neutralized finals.

In Gipuzkoan and Bizkaian areas /f/ is relatively rare and may alternate with /p/; replacement of loan /f/ by /p/ is described as receding in Standard Basque but still reported in recent dialectal loans.
Old Latin/Romance intervocalic /n/ is lost in Basque; Zuberoan may retain nasalized aspiration in some corresponding cases.
In Standard Basque stress/accent is not phonologically contrastive; the widespread pattern places stress on the second syllable, often with secondary prominence on the final syllable.

Basque dialects differ substantially in prosodic systems; the broader literature/source explicitly distinguishes stress-accent systems from pitch-accent/restricted tonal systems in some western dialects, so Standard Basque stress facts must not be generalized to all lects.
